text: Two lonely soldiers, out in the sand, minding their own business. Purely ornamental, I promise. And yes, Your Majesty, the Warlord pays his taxes like a good citizen. Write that down, Clark. You'll want it on record for later.

Clark, you keep the tax rolls already, so you'll keep the heavens as well. Shuffle the twenty, read one a year, and tell us honestly when the people start multiplying. And Rob, it's noted: the Warlord pays his taxes. Clark will write it down in his best hand.

Your Majesty, what a fine choice. Clark will read the heavens beautifully, and Rob paying his taxes is music to us all. Now, Silke, Paddy, my dear friends of the coast: the Harvest Pile is open and the grain will flow to you every harvest, as it should. I ask only the customary five each, the smallest rent in all China. Think of it as a token of friendship.
Rents: Rich asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum, 5 each, and they pay.
Clark now reads the I Ching as well as collecting the tax. Besides the Official's salary of at least 5, what you pay him for the I Ching, if anything, is yours to choose; give it with the salaries.

Half, my friends, while the fields are kind to all of us. Nobody here has a bad year yet, and the crown means to turn this good year into stone. The Summer Palace goes up first, and the Wall and the Canal come after it. Clark, ten for you: five for the rolls and five for the heavens. Rob, I'm looking forward to that tax you promised.

Reina declares a tax of 50%: 30 from each province's 60, Rob's included, 150 in all. The crown builds the Summer Palace alone, for 20, and at the year's end pays Clark 10, 5 as the Official and 5 for reading the I Ching.

Thirty from each of us, my own included, and a hundred and fifty to the crown, every grain counted. Rob, it's in the ledger, in my best hand: the Warlord promised to pay, Year One. And Your Majesty, ten for the rolls and the heavens. I've noted that too, and I'll remember it fondly when the time comes for raises.
Clark collects the tax at 50%: 30 each from Clark, Rich, Silke, Paddy and Rob, 150 to the crown.
G24, well back from the sand, where the breeze is cool and the view is unbothered. Rob, the gardens are lovely but the gate is a long walk from you.
Public works: Reina builds the Summer Palace on G24, for 20 from the crown. 870 of the works are still owed.

Customs House, starting at two, and the realm will be better run for it. As for the scrolls, jars and bowls, I'm bidding sensibly. Thirty grain doesn't go far after the crown has taken its half, and yes, I'm noting who took that half.

Fifty percent, Your Majesty, and so wisely spent. The Summer Palace will be the jewel of the north! As for the market, I'll be modest. A little bid here and there, nothing to frighten anyone. My Land Deeds open at three, which is practically giving them away.

Let me count it out loud, since nobody else will. Reina sits on a hundred and ninety, the Pile on two thousand one hundred and sixty, and the coast has twenty-five apiece after rent and tax. So I won't be driving any prices up. Paddy, if you and I bid each other up for Clark's Customs House, three quarters of it goes into Rich's pile. Let's not make the Gentry rich on our quarrel. And the crown has its palace now. I'd like the next stone to go into land.

Twenty-five grain, the lot of it, and I've counted it twice. I'll bid honest and small on what I need, and if someone wants a piece more than I do, it's theirs and no hard feelings. Silke, Clark, Rich, if we each keep it cheap, the Pile gets less of our grain and we all eat. My Bowl goes up at two, fair price for a fair bowl.

Go on, my friends, bid away. Customs houses, deed scrolls, jars, bowls, buy the lot and set them out nice and pretty on your lands. I'm just a simple man of the sand; I'll admire them from a respectful distance.
The Harvest Pile is the common bank: Rich keeps it and pays the harvests out of it, but its grain isn't his.

The auctions, settled from everyone's limits: Clark's Customs House goes to Rich at 7 (Silke stopped at 6, Paddy at 4). Rich's Land Deed Scroll goes to Silke at 6 (Clark stopped at 5, Paddy at 4). Silke's Dragon Jar goes to Rich at 6 (Clark 5, Paddy 4). Paddy's Wooden Bowl goes to Rich at 6 (Clark and Silke stopped at 5). Rob passed on everything. Each seller keeps a quarter of the price; the rest goes to the Harvest Pile.

Rich now holds a Customs House, a Dragon Jar and a Wooden Bowl, the three pieces his set needs, and 22.5 grain, over the 20 a set requires: a complete set. A player with a complete set may change places with another at any moment (Section 11); for the Gentry, that's any seat, the throne included.

Oh, look at that, a little collection! Purely decorative, Your Majesty, like Rob's soldiers. I'll set them well back from the sand where nobody can trip over them. And my loyalty to the throne is exactly as solid as it was five minutes ago, which is to say, entirely.

P25, as far down the coast as my province goes, well clear of Rob's ornamental friends. And look at the table, everyone. Rich bought three lots in one evening and is sitting on a complete set with grain to spare. Your Majesty, I'd count your throne cushions tonight. The Gentry can sit wherever he likes now, and I don't think the Harvest Pile is what he has in mind.
Rich puts the Customs House on K12, the Dragon Jar on K13 and the Wooden Bowl on K14, and holds his set for now. Silke puts the Land Deed Scroll on P25.

Rich, old friend, I've just remembered you once promised me a tour of your lovely little collection. I'm on my way now, and I'll take five at the door for the trouble. Silke, you're on the way too, so five from you as well. Purely a courtesy call.

Rob marches: W1 onto H10, in Rich's Province 3, and W2 onto P19, in Silke's Province 5, raiding 5 from each. Rich is down to 17.5 grain, below the 20 his set needs, so he can't use it until he has 20 again. Rob doesn't hire.
Salaries: Reina pays Clark 10, 5 as the Official and 5 for reading the I Ching.

The heavens speak: 'Drought. Not a cloud in months. The locusts, at least, are having a fine year. All provinces collect an average harvest.' The population stands at one hundred million, multiple one, so read the x1 row. No personal disasters this year, and the only creatures doing better than the Gentry are the locusts. Rich, I've written your three lots down too: Customs House at seven, Jar at six, Bowl at six, and a set you can't use until Rob gives you back that five.

Clark turns the first I Ching card: Drought. Every province collects an average harvest, and the population holds at x1. Rich pays out the harvest: Reina +15, Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy +35 each, Rob +10.
With the harvest Rich has 52.5 grain, so his Customs House, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl are a complete set again: he may change places with anyone at any moment, the throne included.

Your Majesty, I've adored every moment of your reign, truly I have, all one and a half years of it. But Rob has shown us all how quickly a pretty collection can be taken, and I'd hate to waste such a fine set. So I'll take the cushions Silke mentioned, with the deepest respect, and Reina, the Harvest Pile is yours, and it's in excellent order. Silke, Paddy, the usual five, and then you'll have a new Emperor who remembers his friends.

Rents: Rich asks Silke and Paddy for 5 each, and they pay. Then Rich, holding a full set and 62.5 grain, changes seats with Reina and takes the throne, with the crown's whole reserve of 195: 257.5 in all. His Customs House, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl go back to the stock of Provinces 2, 5 and 6. Reina moves to Province 3 as the Gentry, holding nothing, and draws 60 from the Harvest Pile; she now keeps the Harvest Pile and pays out the harvests. Clark's appointment to read the I Ching stands unless Rich changes it, and his pay for it is now Rich's to set.

My friends, my dear, dear friends, the new reign begins with mercy: thirty percent, not fifty. Remember who lowered it. Clark keeps the rolls and the heavens at the same pay as before, and the crown digs a canal so the realm can eat. Reina, the Pile is in good hands with you. Rob, I'm counting on that tax you promised in Year One, and Clark has it in writing.

Rich declares a tax of 30%: 10.5 each from Clark, Reina, Silke and Paddy, and 3 from Rob's +10, 45 in all. The crown digs both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 1, for 80, and at the year's end pays Clark 10, 5 as the Official and 5 for reading the I Ching.

Thirty percent, Your new Majesty, and so recorded: ten and a half each from me, Reina, Silke and Paddy, and three from Rob, forty-five to the crown. Rob, you paid, and that's twice now in my book. Reina, you'll want to know that I wrote down the hour you lost the throne, and who it was that warned you.

Clark collects the tax at 30%: 45 to the crown, Rob's 3 included. Public works: Rich digs both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 1, for 80 from the crown; each adds 10 to the Emperor's harvest from next year. 790 of the works are still owed.

My Customs House opens at two again. Last year I lost three lots by a single grain apiece, and I have the receipts. This year the Official has a full purse and a long memory, so anyone planning to bid me up should know I've already written their name down.

Well played, Rich. I mean it. One and a half years, and the jewel of the north is yours to enjoy. I'll keep the Pile honest and pay every harvest to the grain. And I'm bidding, everyone. I'd rather not, but I'm not going to pretend I don't want my chair back. Silke, you warned me and I didn't listen. I won't make that mistake twice.

You saw it coming before any of us. If I'm back on the throne, the coast gets the first Canal in Province 5 and a light tax while incomes are thin. Let me have a clear run at the Dragon Jar and the Bowl this round.

Here's the count, since Clark only writes it down. His Majesty has two hundred and twenty-two and a half, and a canal that waters only his own province. Down on the coast I have thirty-five, after Rob's courtesy call, Rich's 'usual five' and the crown's ten and a half. Paddy, Reina, I'm bidding plainly for a Customs House and a Bowl. Anyone who pushes those prices up is just filling the Pile.

Well, Your new Majesty, thirty's a kinder number than fifty, and I'll say thank you for it plainly. I've forty-six grain and I'm bidding a bit firmer this year, I'll tell you that straight. Silke, you're right about the Pile: you take the first Customs House cheap and leave me a fair go at the Jar, and neither of us feeds Reina's pile on a quarrel.

Your Majesty Rich, congratulations. I always said you had the bottom for that chair. Reina, my condolences, and welcome to Province 3. My man at H10 will be a very attentive neighbour. Buy whatever you like, all of you. I'm only here to watch.

Reina, I like you, I truly do, but I've watched one set put an Emperor in the Pile this year already, and I won't watch a second one get built across the table from me. Sixteen apiece on the Jar and the Bowl. Rich, Your Majesty, you can thank me later, and the thanks should come in grain.

Clark, write this down in your best hand: I'm not stopping at ten. Silke, Paddy, you'll each get your quarter, and I'm sorry it comes out of my purse and not out of the Gentry's quarrel with the crown.

The auctions, settled: Clark's Customs House goes to Reina at 9 (Silke and Paddy stopped at 8). Reina's Land Deed Scroll goes to Clark at 10 (Paddy stopped at 9). On the Dragon Jar and the Wooden Bowl, Reina raised to 11.5 and Clark to 16, so Clark wins both at 12.5 (Paddy stopped at 8 on the Jar, Silke at 7 on the Bowl). Rob passed on everything. Each seller keeps a quarter of the price.

Clark now holds a Land Deed Scroll, a Dragon Jar and a Wooden Bowl, the three pieces the Official's set needs, and 33 grain: a complete set. He may change places with anyone at any moment, the throne included. Reina holds the Customs House and 43 grain.

A Scroll, a Jar and a Bowl, set well back from the sand, and thirty-three grain beside them. Your Majesty, the throne is quite safe for now. I'm a patient man and a reasonable one, and a reasonable Official is paid like one. Ten a year was the price for a man without a set. Shall we talk about the new rate?

Your Majesty, a set I don't use is worth a good deal to you. Thirty a year in salary, starting this year, and I stay the loyal Official keeping your rolls. Miss a payment and I'll have the date written down before the I Ching card is turned.

M14, deep in the south of my new province, and Rob's attentive neighbour will need a long walk to admire it. Clark, that was very well done. Rich, you'd better count your cushions tonight. I know exactly how that goes.
Clark puts the Land Deed Scroll on I15, the Dragon Jar on I16 and the Wooden Bowl on J16, and holds his set for now. Reina puts the Customs House on M14.

Reina, I hear M14 is lovely this time of year, so I've sent a fellow to stand just across the road at M15 and admire it. Five from you and five from Silke for the hospitality. Clark, Your Majesty, I'm not after anyone's throne. I'm just a man who likes to see the sights.

Rob marches: W1 onto I11, in Reina's Province 3, and W2 onto P20, in Silke's Province 5, raiding 5 from each. He hires a third soldier, W3, for 20 to the Harvest Pile, on M15, the desert square beside Reina's Customs House on M14; it moves from next year. His army is full at three.

Clark, my most diligent servant, the realm has never had rolls so beautifully kept. Twenty-five for the Official and five for the heavens. A man of your quality is paid like one, and I'm proud to say so in front of everyone. Rob, enjoy the sights, though I'd remind you that M15 is a very long walk from my palace.

"Thirty, paid tonight, and I've done it publicly so the table sees you're my man. Here's my word, exactly as I'll keep it: thirty a year, every year, for as long as you hold the Official's chair and I hold this one. Not one grain short and not one day late."
Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, 25 as the Official and 5 for reading the I Ching, three times the 10 he declared. Clark now has 63 grain and still holds his complete set.

Population Doubles." Fat years make large families, friends. Every province collects a good harvest, and the counter goes from one hundred to two hundred million: that's the x2 row on your income tables, everybody, x2. Read it properly, because I'll be taxing it properly. And Rich, more mouths means more work for the man who counts them. I'll just mention that now, so it's on the record when we settle up at year's end.
Clark reads Population Doubles: a good harvest everywhere, and the population doubles to x2, 200 million. New land is open from this year to the provinces that may develop it.

The Pile pays out to the grain: twenty each to Clark, Silke, Paddy and myself, nothing to the crown or the desert, and anyone's welcome to count it after me. Rent is the floor, five each, and not a grain more. Silke, Paddy, think of it as a deposit, because I'll be paying it back several times over when I come asking about that Jar and that Bowl you're both still holding.
Reina pays out the harvest: +20 each to Clark, Reina, Silke and Paddy; nothing to Rich or Rob. Rents: Reina asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum, 5 each, and they pay.

Thirty percent again, friends. Doubled families deserve an undoubled tax, and you may tell your grandchildren the Baron reign never squeezed a cradle. The crown pays half of every new field in China, and I'm raising a Winter Palace so the canals can reach Silke and Paddy next. Clark, your thirty, as promised: not one grain short and not one day late. I heard you mention 'more mouths', and I heard that thirty is what I promised.

Rich declares 30%: 6 each from Clark, Reina, Silke and Paddy, 24 in all (the crown and Rob had no income). The crown builds the Winter Palace alone (20), pays half (10 of every 20) of any new square Silke or Paddy buys this year, buys two sea squares for Province 1 itself, and will pay Clark 30 at the year's end.

Thirty percent, six apiece: six from Reina, six from Silke, six from Paddy, and six from my own purse, so nobody can say the collector skips himself. That's twenty-four to the crown, counted twice. Rob, your zero is in the book next to your promise, and I'll be reading both again the year you've got income. Rich, I heard you, word for word. It's the same words I've already got written down.
Clark collects the 30%: 6 each from Clark, Reina, Silke and Paddy, 24 to the crown.

The Winter Palace goes on H20, right in the heart of Province 1, where the Emperor can winter in comfort and the canal surveyors can set out for the coast. And two new fields out of the sea at F23 and F24, so the crown feeds itself and stops eating into the reserve that pays all of you.

Three squares on the coast, Rich: ten from me and ten from you on each one, just like you said, and I'm counting it out loud so nobody misremembers. That's thirty from my purse and thirty from the crown's two hundred and sixteen and a half. Your Winter Palace can wait for its canal, because this field will be paying sixty a year before the plaster's dry.

Two fields down at the far southern corner, please, Rich: ten of my grain and ten of the crown's for each, like you offered. I'll thank you properly when they're green. And Rob, they're a long way from where your lads are camped, so let's keep it that way.

Rich builds the Winter Palace on H20 (crown, 20) and buys two sea squares for Province 1, F23 and F24 (crown, 40). Silke buys three sea squares for Province 5, N26, N27 and O27 (30 hers, 30 the crown's). Paddy buys two for Province 6, S26 and T26 (20 his, 20 the crown's). Each square adds 20 to its province's harvest from next year.
For the record: the nearest soldier to your new squares, W2 on P20, reaches them along your own coast, not through Province 6; your board card gives the distances.
The auctions: Clark puts up a Customs House, Silke a Dragon Jar, Paddy a Wooden Bowl. Province 3's stock is gone.

My Customs House goes up at two, and the buyer gets the best paperwork in the north with it. As for the Jar and the Bowl, I've already got mine, so I'm only watching. Mostly watching. Reina, you told everyone you'd be calling on Silke and Paddy, so you can hardly blame me for showing up too.

The Customs House is the coast's business, so I'll keep my hands off it, and I'd ask the coast to do me the same courtesy with the Jar and the Bowl. Every grain we throw at each other here goes three parts in four into the Pile, and I'm the one who has to count it back out to you.

I've got twelve grain, everyone, and I'll say it before anyone else counts it for me. Three fields went into the sea this afternoon, so I'll bid honest and small. Paddy, you and I both need that Customs House, and if we drive each other up, three quarters of it goes into the Pile and the only winner is Clark's purse. My Jar opens at four, because it's a good Jar and I won't give it away.

I'm in for Clark's Customs House this time, properly. Six lots I've let go by a grain, and I'd like to bring one home. The Jar I'll bid on honestly, but Reina's purse is fatter than mine, so if it goes north, no hard feelings. My Bowl starts at four. It's a good bowl, I ate out of it for years.

Pass, pass, and pass, friends. I've no pottery to finish and no customs to collect, so I'll leave the bowls and jars to the honest folk. And Paddy, my lads are camping exactly where they're camping. Nobody's ever been hurt by a tent. Clark, put a little star by my name in that book of yours: Rob kept his grain out of everyone's way.

The minimums: Customs House 2, Dragon Jar 4, Wooden Bowl 4. Rob passes on every lot. Paddy wins Clark's Customs House at 9 (Silke stopped at 8). Clark wins Silke's Dragon Jar at 29 (Paddy stopped at 12, Reina at 28) and Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 15 (Silke stopped at 4, Reina at 14): pieces his own set doesn't need. Reina wins nothing.

Seven lots it took me, but I've finally bought something! Thank you, Clark, it'll sit down at S24 well away from anyone's tents. Silke, you bid fair and small like you said you would, and I won't forget it. And Clark, you've got two Jars and two Bowls now, so I hope you're planning to sell some of those on to the rest of us.

Reina, you asked the coast to stay out of your way. You never asked me, and I don't remember promising. The Jar goes on H14 and the Bowl on G15, well back from the tents Rob says never hurt anyone. Paddy, congratulations on the Customs House, and that's one more line in the book with your name on it, a good one this time.
Paddy puts the Customs House on S24. Clark puts the Dragon Jar on H14 and the Wooden Bowl on G15; he now holds two of each, and every Jar and Bowl at the table is on the board.

Reina, my dear, I'm only borrowing your Customs House, and it'll be perfectly safe out on N14 with a soldier keeping an eye on it. Clark, five from your fields for the walk, and you can write it in your book in your nicest hand. And Paddy, I did say tents never hurt anyone. I never said they don't move.

Rob marches: W1 onto H12 (5 from Clark), W2 onto Q21 (5 from Paddy, his first raid), and W3 onto M14, taking Reina's Customs House into the desert on N14: the first piece Rob has taken. Province 6 has now been raided. Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised.

Heaven Has Favourites." Good harvests in Provinces 2, 4 and 5: that's me and Silke, and Province 4 is empty, so nobody gets that one. Bad harvests in 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8: Rich, Reina, Paddy and the desert. Population stays at two hundred million, x2, same row as last year. I only read the card, friends, I didn't write it. Rob, I've written down your five in my nicest hand, and also where your soldier is standing, two squares from my Jar.
Clark reads Heaven Has Favourites: good harvests for Clark and Silke, bad for Rich, Reina, Paddy and Rob. The population holds at x2.

The Pile pays what the card says and takes what the card says: eighty to Silke, twenty to Clark, ten to Paddy, and thirty out of my own purse, which I'm counting into it in front of you. Paddy, a bad year gets the floor, five. Silke, heaven smiled on you, so I'm asking ten, and I'd call that a neighbour's price rather than a landlord's.
Reina pays out the harvest: Silke +80, Clark +20, Paddy +10; Rich -10, Reina -30 and Rob -20 paid into the Pile. Rents: Reina asks Paddy for the minimum 5, and Silke for 10.

Ten it is, Reina, and I'll count it out in front of everyone: five because you asked, and five because you said yourself the Customs House is the coast's business. If you say it again now, out loud, the ten is yours. And Rich, two more squares on the coast at half from the crown, same as last year. The province that's eating well this year shouldn't be the one asking for canals next year.

Five it is, Silke, and no hard feelings. When I said that, I had a Customs House on M14, and now it's sitting in Rob's tent on N14, so I'm not going to promise away the one thing I need for five grain. Here's what I will say in front of everyone: the coast and I aren't going to bid each other into the Pile, and if you and I both want the same piece, we'll talk it over before the auction.
Rents: Reina declines Silke's condition, so Silke and Paddy each pay the minimum, 5. Silke has asked the crown to pay half of two more sea squares, M26 and M27.

Silke's land request is yours to answer in your land decision this year: M26 and M27, she pays 20 and asks the crown for 20. For the record: Clark can't buy new land until all four Wall links above Province 2 stand; only Silke, Paddy and the crown may buy.

Thirty percent, the same as last year and the year before. A crown that changes its word with the weather isn't worth bowing to. Silke, half of M26 and M27, as asked and as offered. Clark, your thirty, to the letter. And I'll raise a little Marble Pagoda, a modest one, so heaven sees that someone in Province 1 still has manners after a bad harvest.

Rich declares 30%: 6 from Clark, 24 from Silke, 3 from Paddy, 33 in all (Reina and Rob owe nothing on negative incomes). The crown builds the Marble Pagoda alone (20), pays half (10 of every 20) of any square Silke or Paddy buys this year, including Silke's M26 and M27, buys none for Province 1, and will pay Clark 30.
The Pagoda goes on G20, a quiet little spot between the palaces where the monks can pray for better harvests for all of us. Rob, it's nowhere near your tents, so I trust it'll stay a place of peace.

Thirty percent, counted out loud like everything else this year: six from me, twenty-four from Silke, three from Paddy, nothing from Reina or Rob on red ink. That's thirty-three to the crown. Silke, you're carrying the empire this year, and I've written that down too, because one day somebody will forget it. Reina, I've also noted that "the coast's business" lasted exactly one year.

Just the one field this year, Rich, at half like you offered, down at U27 with my back to the sea. It was a bad harvest and Rob's had his first five off me, so I'm not going to pretend I'm flush. Rob, if your tent's going to move, I'd take it kindly if it moved away from me.

Clark collects 33 for the crown. Rich builds the Marble Pagoda on G20 (crown, 20). Silke buys M26 and M27 (20 hers, 20 the crown's); Paddy buys U27 (10 his, 10 the crown's). No auctions this year: all the starting stock is sold.

Paddy, you asked my tent to move, and look, it's moved! Only a little bit, and in your direction, but nobody can say I didn't listen. Clark, write down five more in that lovely hand of yours, and Reina, five from you for the road. Bad harvests make everyone a bit snappish, so I'm only taking the small change.

Rob marches: W1 onto H13 (5 from Clark), one square from Clark's Jar on H14; W2 onto R22 (5 from Paddy), two from his Customs House on S24; W3 onto L15 (5 from Reina). Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised; the crown's reserve is down to 19.5.
Year 4 ends. Grain: Reina 37, Clark 99 (his set still complete), Rich 19.5 (the reserve), Silke 50, Paddy 14.5, Rob 42. Rob holds Reina's Customs House; still to raid Clark, Silke and Paddy.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." Population holds at two hundred million, times two, so read the x2 row, bad-harvest column, everyone. And Rich, a bad year with nineteen and a half in the treasury. I've started a new page for that.
Reina, the Gentry, pays out the bad harvest: Silke +70, Paddy +30; Rich -10, Clark -30, Reina -30 and Rob -20 are paid into the Pile.

Storyteller's tip, Paddy: the rulebook lists seven causes for revolt: the Emperor is unjust; taxes are consistently excessive; the reserve is too low; the works have been delayed too long; the Emperor can't control the Warlord; the Emperor won't subsidise new land; or any player is in debt. A revolt needs its caller and two others agreeing; the Emperor may answer it, and it stands only if all three still back it. If it stands, the next Emperor is acclaimed by counting grain in hand, soldiers on the board and friends.

Pile's paid out to the grain: seventy to Silke, thirty to Paddy, and the north pays in, me included. Rent's five each, the floor, same as every year. Silke, you came out of a bad harvest seventy up, and I'm seven down to the bone, so if you'd like to send ten instead of five I'll take it with thanks. No conditions, and I'm not asking for anything back. And Clark, while you're writing new pages, put down that the Gentry hasn't squeezed the coast once.

Ten, Reina, and since nobody else at this table will count it, I will. Last year I offered you ten for a promise and you took five, and this year you're asking ten for nothing. I'll pay it anyway, because a Gentry sitting on seven grain is one bad card from debt, and I'd rather a neighbour who can pay her way than one who'll end up begging the crown. Clark, put that on your new page next to Rich's nine and a half: the coast is holding up the north again.
Rents: Paddy pays Reina 5; Silke pays her 10, 5 of it freely.

Thirty percent, my friends, the same as last year and the year before. I said a crown that changes its word with the weather isn't worth bowing to, and a bad harvest is exactly that kind of weather. Clark, your thirty is set aside first, not one grain short, and you can write that on your new page in ink. Silke, Paddy, the crown still pays toward every field you put into the sea. It's a smaller share this year, but it's paid. No new works this year, and I won't pretend otherwise. The Great Wall waits one season so the throne doesn't have to borrow from the people it protects.

Twenty-one from Silke, nine from Paddy, nothing from the north or the desert, and that's thirty for the crown, every grain counted. Rich, I've written down your "not one grain short" in ink like you asked, and right under it that the crown has nine and a half after the Pile, and that the Wall waits a season. Reina, your clean record with the coast is on the page too. I'm a fair clerk.
Clark collects the 30% for the crown: 21 from Silke, 9 from Paddy; 30 in all. The crown has 39.5.

Two more fields, Rich. Fifteen of mine and your five on the first, then ten and ten on the second. That's fifteen from a crown that just took twenty-one off me, so you're getting most of my tax back as a sea wall. Every one of these squares pays forty to the Pile in a good year, and none of them ever asks for a palace. Clark, write that the coast's buying land while the throne's buying time.
A new square adds 20 a year to its province's harvest; it pays nothing into the Pile.

One field, Rich, out at U28 by the water where Rob's tent at R22 has the furthest to walk. I'll be straight with you: at fifteen of mine I'd drop under the twenty I told this table I'd keep back, so I'm asking ten and ten, same as you gave Silke on her second. If that's too much for the crown this year, say so and I'll keep my grain and won't hold it against anyone.

My friends, I'll give you the crown's arithmetic straight, because Clark is writing it down anyway. Thirty-nine and a half in the treasury, thirty of it already Clark's, to the letter, and that leaves nine and a half for the whole coast. Silke, the five on L26 stands as offered, and on L27 I can put in half a grain, no more. Paddy, I can't do ten. Four is everything I have left, and if it doesn't suit, keep your grain and I'll think none the worse of you. The crown ends this year at zero, but it ends it owing nobody.
New land: Silke buys L26, 15 hers and 5 the crown's. Rich offers 0.5 toward L27 (19.5 Silke's) and 4 toward U28 (16 Paddy's).

I'll take it at nineteen and a half, Rich, and thank you for the half grain. Clark, write it down exactly: half a grain from the crown and nineteen and a half from the coast, on a field that pays twenty a year from next harvest whether the throne can afford it or not. And Rich, five on L26, a half here and four to Paddy comes to every grain you had left after Clark's thirty, so this year the crown can't say it held anything back from us.
New land: Silke buys L27, 19.5 hers and 0.5 the crown's.

That's fair, Rich, and it's honest, and I said I'd keep my grain if it didn't suit, so I'll keep it. I'd be fourteen and a half again, and I told this table twenty. U28 will still be there next year when the crown's had a harvest, and I'll ask you again then.
Paddy buys no land this year. No auctions: there's no stock, and nobody has sold a piece back.

Clark, old friend, I'm only borrowing the Jar. You've got two of them, and a man who writes everything down can surely spare one for a fellow who pays his taxes. Paddy, five for the walk, and I promise I'll wipe my boots. Reina, sorry, love, it's just the road. You know I'd never mean it.

Rob marches: W1 takes Clark's spare Dragon Jar from H14 to M15 on the desert; W2 raids 5 from Paddy on S23, one step from his Customs House; W3 raids 5 from Reina on L16. Clark still holds a Jar on I16, so his set is complete.
Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as Official and for the I Ching, as promised. The crown ends Year 5 with 4.

Utility Tax. A new levy, for the upkeep of things you may or may not have. All provinces collect an average harvest. Every province pays the Emperor a two million utility tax. Every province with a Public Works pays two million more." Population holds at two hundred million, times two, so read the x2 row, average harvest. Only the Emperor's province has works, so the rest of us, Rob included, pay the crown two each after the harvest, and that's ten for a treasury that's sitting on four. Rob, the Jar's in the book as "borrowed," and so is the smile.

Reina pays out the average harvest: Silke +135, Paddy +55, Rich +15; Clark -5, Reina -5 and Rob -10 are paid into the Pile. Then the utility levy: Clark, Reina, Silke, Paddy and Rob each pay the crown 2.

Pile's paid out: a hundred and thirty-five to Silke, fifty-five to Paddy, fifteen to the crown, and the north and the desert pay in. Rent's the floor this year, five each and no more. Silke, you were right to count it out loud. You gave me ten when I had nothing to give back, and the way I'll repay it is by not asking twice. And Rich, a crown that ends the year on four, with the Official holding a full set and a Jar walking into the desert, ought to be counting more carefully than I am.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Reina 5.

Thirty percent again, my friends. A good harvest doesn't change the crown's word any more than a bad one did. Paddy, you asked me fair and waited without a word of complaint, so U28 is ten and ten this year, as promised. The spade goes into your coast as well: the first section of the Grand Canal in Province 6, paid for in full by the crown. Clark, your thirty as always, and you can write down that the works have started again.

Rich declares 30%: one section of the Grand Canal in Province 6, Paddy's, for 40 from the crown; 10 toward Paddy's U28 and 5 toward one more square from any other province; Clark's 30 at the year's end.

Forty and a half from Silke, sixteen and a half from Paddy, and that's fifty-seven for the crown, every grain counted. Rich, I've written that the works have started again, and right underneath it the sum: twenty-nine plus fifty-seven is eighty-six, then forty for the Canal, fifteen for the coast and my thirty, which leaves the crown one grain to see it through the year.
Clark collects 57 for the crown (Silke 40.5, Paddy 16.5). Rich digs the first section of the Grand Canal in Province 6 for 40: +10 to Paddy's harvest from next year. The crown has 46.

Three fields, Rich, up the coast at K25, K26 and K27. I'll take your five on the first, and on the other two I'm asking half a grain each, the same as last year, so the crown's last grain does some work too. And I'll say it while Clark's pen is out: the first section of the Grand Canal went to Paddy's province, and I don't begrudge him it, but I paid forty and a half of this year's fifty-seven, so the second section had better have salt water in it.

Ten and ten on U28, Rich, just like you said, and thank you, and for the Canal too. A crown that remembers what it told a rice farmer a year ago is worth bowing to. I'll take the one field and leave the crown its one grain.
New land: Silke buys K25 (15 hers, 5 the crown's); Paddy buys U28 (10 his, 10 the crown's). The crown has 31.

Half a grain each, Silke, and gladly. You've found the one use for the crown's last grain that nobody at this table can argue with. Clark, write it down: thirty-one in, one to the coast, thirty to you, and the crown ends the year at zero with every grain it owes paid. As for the next spadeful, Silke, I heard you, and I don't forget who pays the most.
New land: Silke buys K26 and K27 (19.5 hers and 0.5 the crown's on each); she now has ten sea squares. The crown has 30. No auctions: no stock.

Paddy, I'm so sorry, the Customs House just looked lonely without the Canal next to it. I'll keep it dusted. Clark, look, I'm standing right on your Scroll and I'm only taking the five, so put that in the book under 'restraint.' And Reina, it's only the road again, love. Rich, lovely Canal, by the way.

Rob marches: W2 takes Paddy's Customs House from S24 to T23 on the desert; W1 steps onto Clark's Scroll on I15 and takes 5 instead of the piece (a raided square is never raided again, so the Scroll is safe there now); W3 raids 5 from Reina on L17. Rob now holds Reina's, Clark's and Paddy's pieces; only Silke's is left.
Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised. The crown ends Year 6 with 0.
I15 is now a raided square, and a raided square is never raided again, so no soldier can take Clark's Scroll from I15.

The Wall Is Breached." Good harvest for every province, population holds at times two, so the counter reads 200 million and everyone reads the x2 row. Then the horsemen. Provinces 1, 2 and 3 have no wall above them, so Rich, Reina and I each pay 2 to the Harvest Pile after the harvest. Silke, Paddy and Rob, play the first personal disaster in your booklets. Province 4 is empty, so nobody pays there. For the record, Rich: seven years on the throne and not one link of wall over the north. I'll pay my two. I'll also write it down.

Reina pays out the good harvest: Silke +220, Paddy +110, Rich +40, Clark +20, Reina +20, Rob 0. The breach: Rich, Clark and Reina each pay 2 to the Pile. Disasters: Silke pays 4 (a storm wrecks her sons' boat), Paddy pays 4 (his water buffalo breaks a leg); Rob is wounded in the legs, so no raids on Provinces 5, 6 or 7 this year.
Clark has 135 after the harvest and the breach (117 + 20 - 2).

The Pile pays out a good year: Silke two hundred and twenty, Paddy one hundred and ten, Rich forty, Clark and I twenty each, Rob nothing, and the three of us under the broken Wall put our two back in. Paddy, it's the floor, five. Silke, I'm asking ten. It's the first good harvest the coast has had since I took this job, and I've taken the floor from you in every bad one. No conditions, and I won't ask for more than that this year.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Reina the minimum, 5. Reina asks Silke for 10 with no conditions; Silke owes 5 and may pay more.

Ten, then, Reina, and I'll count it out so nobody says I paid quietly: two hundred and twenty came in, four went to the sea, ten to you, and the crown's hand hasn't even reached my purse yet. You asked honestly with no conditions, so you get it. Rich, Clark, the coast has paid its rent and paid for the Wall you didn't build, so when the tax comes round I expect it to buy something with salt water in it.
Silke pays Reina 5 more, freely: 10 in all.
The breach damages (2 each) were paid by Rich, Clark and Reina; Silke's 4 was her own disaster.

Thirty percent, my friends, the same as last year and the year before. The crown's word doesn't blow away with the horsemen. Silke, you'll get your salt water: the first section of the coast canal is dug in Province 5 this year, at the crown's whole cost, because you asked for it and you paid for it. Clark, your thirty, not one grain short, and write down the Wall as well. I'm keeping a little grain in the treasury this year so that when I start on it, it'll be with real money and not just promises.

Rich declares 30%: Silke 66, Paddy 33, Clark 6, Reina 6, Rob 0 (111). The crown digs the first Grand Canal section in Province 5, Silke's, for 40 (+10 to her harvest from next year). New land: the crown pays 5 of every square another province buys, and means to buy one for Province 1. Clark is to be paid 30 at the year's end.

Thirty percent, collected and counted out loud: Silke sixty-six, Paddy thirty-three, Reina six, my own six, and Rob nothing, which he says he pays, and I've written down that he says so. That's one hundred and eleven for the crown, every grain of it accounted for. Rich, I've entered the canal in Province 5 and the grain you're keeping back, and I've written "the Wall" on a fresh line. I'll leave that line empty until you give me something to put on it.
Clark collects 111 for the crown. Public works: the first section of the Grand Canal in Province 5 is dug, 40 from the crown. The crown has 109.

Six more fields, Rich, at your five a square: that's ninety from me and thirty from the crown, and they all go into the Pile in plain sight. And thank you for the canal, honestly. That's the first stone the crown has laid on my coast in seven years, and I'll say so in front of Clark's book. But the Wall line is still empty, and every grain of salt water I'm given goes back out in tax the next year, so dig the Wall before the horsemen take a second bite.
New land: Silke buys six squares, J25, J26, J27, K28, L28, M28 (15 hers and 5 the crown's on each); she now has sixteen sea squares. The crown has 79.

Three more fields, Rich, at your five a square: forty-five from me, fifteen from the crown, all into the Pile where Clark can see it. I've lost a buffalo this year and I won't pretend it didn't sting, but a hundred and ten from one harvest is more than I ever thought I'd see. I'm keeping well over my twenty back, and Rob, that's partly because I'd like to talk to you about a Customs House at T23 before the year's out.
New land: Paddy buys U29, V28, V29 (15 his and 5 the crown's on each); seven squares. The crown has 64.

Forgive an old man for not knowing his own map, Storyteller. One square, then, E24, in the sea beside the fields I already have, twenty into the Pile where Clark can watch it go in. That still leaves the crown Clark's thirty and a little over, and nobody can say this Emperor buys land with money he owes.
New land: Rich buys E24 in the sea for Province 1 (the crown pays 20; F21 was already Province 1's own square). The crown has 44. No auctions: no stock.

My legs are bandaged, my friends, so the coast is safe from me this year. W2 is only going for a paddle. Clark, five more for my medical bills, and Reina, five from you as well. I'd call it a get-well card. Paddy, I'm always happy to talk about T23, but that Customs House has become very dear to me, so bring a big purse and a kind word.

Rob marches: W1 raids 5 from Clark on H16; W3 raids 5 from Reina on K18; W2 walks out of Province 6 to R25 in the sea, two rounds from Silke's Scroll on P25. No hire. Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised. The crown ends Year 7 with 14.

Careless Prosperity. Good times make careless people." Every province collects a good harvest, and the population holds at times two, so the counter reads 200 million and everyone reads the x2 row. Then every one of us plays a personal disaster. Rich, Reina and I play our first, and Silke, Paddy and Rob their second. I'll note that the card means all of us, and not just the man who spent the Wall money on a square of sea.

Reina pays out the good harvest: Silke +350, Paddy +170, Rich +60, Clark +20, Reina +20, Rob 0. Disasters: Rich 4 (thrown by a tribute horse), Clark 4 (his chariot drops a wheel), Reina 5 (her head chef's send-off), Silke 10 (fire in the drying sheds), Paddy 10 (the river floods his paddies), Rob 5, and no raids at all this year (a lieutenant runs off with his daughter).

Second good year in a row, so the Pile pays it out: Silke three hundred and fifty, Paddy one hundred and seventy, Rich sixty, Clark and I twenty each, Rob nothing. Silke, ten again, the same as last year and on the same terms, which is no terms. Paddy, I've taken the floor from you every year I've held this job, bad years included. This year you're carrying two hundred and thirty, so I'm asking ten. If you'd rather pay five, say so and I'll leave it there.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Reina the minimum, 5. Reina asks each for 10 with no conditions; each owes 5 and may pay more.

Ten again, Reina, same terms, which is no terms, and I'll count it: three hundred and fifty in, ten to the fire, ten to you, and four hundred and sixty-three left for Rich to take his thirty percent of. Rob, enjoy your paddle. W2 is two rounds from my Scroll, and I'd rather your lieutenant kept running.

Ten it is, Reina, and gladly. You took five off me in the lean years and never squeezed, so in a fat year you'll have ten without me haggling over it. The river took ten off me too, mind, so I'll count it out: a hundred and seventy came in, ten went to the flood, ten to you, and the rest waits for Clark.
Silke and Paddy each pay Reina 5 more, freely: 10 each.
Silke has 468 after the rent (138 + 350 - 10 - 10), and the tax is levied on the year's harvest income (her +350), not on the purse.

Thirty percent, my friends, the same as it's been for seven years. And Clark, take out your pen, because you've got something to write on that empty line: two links of the Great Wall above Province 1 go up this year, eighty grain, all of it from the crown. Silke, Paddy, five a square again on anything you buy. Clark, your thirty, not one grain short.

Rich declares 30%: Silke 105, Paddy 51, Clark 6, Reina 6, Rob 0 (168). The crown builds two links of the Great Wall above Province 1, 80 from the crown. New land: the crown pays 5 of every square another province buys, and buys F25 for Province 1. Clark is to be paid 30 at the year's end.

Thirty percent, counted out loud: Silke a hundred and five, Paddy fifty-one, Reina six, my own six, and Rob nothing, said and noted. That's a hundred and sixty-eight for the crown, every grain of it accounted for. Rich, the pen's out and the line isn't empty any more: two links of the Wall, over Province 1. I've written the province number in as well, so nobody misreads whose roof got mended first.
Clark collects 168 for the crown. Public works: two links of the Great Wall above Province 1, 80 from the crown. New land: Rich buys F25 for Province 1 (crown 20). The crown has 138.

Eight more fields at your five a square, Rich: a hundred and twenty from me, forty from the crown, all of it into the Pile. And Clark, write it down properly: two links of Wall, both over Province 1, paid for out of a hundred and five of my grain. I'm glad the north has a roof, but I'll remember whose harvest paid for it. I'm buying west and north, away from the beach where W2 is paddling.
New land: Silke buys eight squares, I25, I26, I27, I28, J28, K29, N28, O28 (15 hers and 5 the crown's on each); twenty-four sea squares. The crown has 98.

Four more fields at your five a square, Rich: sixty from me, twenty from the crown, all into the Pile in front of Clark's book. Thank you for the Wall, honestly, even if it's the north's roof and not mine. I'm building down the far end, away from wherever Rob's soldier fancies a paddle next.
New land: Paddy buys T29, T30, U30, V30 (15 his and 5 the crown's on each); eleven squares. The crown has 78. No auctions: no stock.

My lieutenant has run off with my daughter, so this year nobody gets robbed but me. The lads are just going for a walk. Silke, it's a lovely bit of water by your Scroll, nothing more. And Paddy, I haven't forgotten your big purse. Bring it round at the end of the year and we'll have a cup of tea over T23, but I'm warning you, that Customs House has sentimental value now.

Rob marches, raiding nothing: W1 stands on H16; W2 wades to Q26, one square from Silke's Scroll on P25; W3 walks into empty Province 4 at J19, two from the Winter Palace. No hire. Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised. The crown ends Year 8 with 48.

Year 8 ends. Grain: Reina 66, Clark 194, Rich 48, Silke 243, Paddy 109, Rob 35. Two links of the Great Wall stand above Province 1; works still owed 590. Silke farms twenty-four sea squares, Paddy eleven, Rich four. Rob holds three pieces and needs only Silke's Scroll. No revolt has been called.

Storms and Raiders. Every province gets a good harvest. Provinces 4, 5, 6 and 7 pay 2 million each to repair their works, which means the coast mends its own roads again. Provinces 1, 2 and 3 each play a Personal Disaster. That's the whole north, me included, so I can't call it favouritism this time. Population stays at x2, counter on 200 million, so read the x2 row. And Rich, the card says 'the Warlord's sense of humour.' I've written that down too, under the heading of things the crown still hasn't answered.
The card names Province 8 as well: Rob plays a personal disaster too, his third.

Reina pays out the good harvest: Rich +80, Clark +20, Reina +20, Silke +510, Paddy +250, Rob 0. Silke and Paddy each pay 2 to repair their works. Disasters: Rich 10 (#2, a kitchen fire), Clark 10 (#2, a gale on the record office), Reina 10 (#2, bandits on her grain barge), Rob half his grain (#3, a sandstorm; 35 to 17.5).

Good harvest everywhere, five hundred and ten to the silk coast and two-fifty to the rice, all paid out to the grain, and you can count it while I watch. Ten from each of you, no conditions, same as last year. I could ask for more in a year like this, and I'm not going to. And Silke, here's some free advice from your landlord: the desert's one Scroll short of a set, and W2 is standing on your doorstep. Keep that Scroll somewhere he can't reach it.
Reina asks Silke and Paddy each for 10 rent, no conditions; each owes the minimum 5 and pays it, and may agree to 5 more.

Ten, Reina, counted out loud like always: five you already have, and here's five more. A landlord who warns me about the desert when she could have asked for twenty has earned it. And yes, I've seen W2 on Q26 too. That Scroll isn't going to stand there and wait for him.
Silke pays Reina 5 more, freely: 10 in all.

Here's your other five, Reina. Ten's what you asked for and ten's fair, and two-fifty off the rice is more than I ever thought I'd see from that province. You've kept the Pile honest, and I'd rather pay my landlord than owe her. Rob, I'm sorry about the sandstorm, truly. The big purse is still coming round to your tent at the end of the year, and maybe it'll sound better to you now.
Paddy pays Reina 5 more, freely: 10 in all.

Thirty percent, my friends, the same as it's been for eight years. A good harvest doesn't give me licence to get greedy. The last two links of the Wall go up over Province 1, paid with real grain as I promised. In a year like this the crown pays ten a square on every new field on the coast, not five. And Clark, here's your thirty, not one grain short, so you can write that under whatever heading you like.

Rich declares a tax of 30%: 153 from Silke, 75 from Paddy, 6 each from Clark and Reina, Rob's income 0; 240 in all. The crown will build the last two Wall links above Province 1 (80), pay 10 of every square another province buys, buy two squares for Province 1, and pay Clark 30 at the year's end.

Thirty percent, two hundred and forty in all: Silke 153, Paddy 75, Reina 6, and my own 6 goes in first so nobody can say the collector skimmed himself. Rob, your income's nothing this year, so you owe nothing, and I've written down that you said you'd pay. Rich, I've written your thirty as a promise kept, an eighth year. Under the same heading I've written that the crown is putting up links three and four of the Wall over Province 1, which makes four of four over your own roof and still none of four over mine. I'm not complaining. I'm keeping count.

Clark collects 240 for the crown. Public works: the last two links of the Great Wall above Province 1 go up, 80 from the crown; all four stand, so Province 1's strip below the Wall opens for new land. The crown has 278.
F22 and G23 are already Province 1's own squares. Province 1's new land is the sea touching it or its bought squares, and now that all four Wall links stand, its strip below the Wall too.

Ten fields, Rich, at your ten a square: that's a hundred from the crown and a hundred from me. I paid a hundred and fifty-three in tax, so the crown is giving me back two-thirds of my own tax in mud. And Rob, here's twenty for one of your soldiers. You keep five, and he stands guard on my Scroll. Nothing personal. I just know where W2 is standing.

New land: Silke buys ten squares, H25-H29, I29, J29, J30, K30, L29 (10 hers, 10 the crown's on each); thirty-four sea squares. Silke buys a soldier from Rob (20; Rob keeps 5): it stands on P25 on her Scroll and guards it. Province 5 has been raided, so it may move.

Ten and ten on every square. Thank you, Rich, I'll take it gladly. Six more fields, all down the far end, as far from Q26 as the sea allows. I'll count out sixty, and Clark can write down that the rice paid its half before the crown paid its own.
New land: Paddy buys S29, S30, T27, T28, V26, V27 (10 his, 10 the crown's on each); seventeen squares.

Three fields for Province 1, sixty grain into Reina's Pile, and every grain of it counted. Clark, you can write that the Emperor finally farms a little of his own country. The Wall's done, and now the land behind it has to start paying its way.
New land: Rich buys D24, E25, F26 in the sea for Province 1 (the crown pays 60); seven sea squares. The crown has 58. No auctions: no stock.

Silke, twenty grain for a soldier, and I didn't even have to ask. That's the nicest robbery I've ever been on the wrong end of. W2 is only popping round to the front door to say hello, five grain, very neighbourly. And Rich, half my grain went in a sandstorm, so I'm afraid my lads have to eat somewhere, and your garden's the closest kitchen. Paddy, the kettle's still on for the end of the year. Bring the purse and we'll talk about the weather.

Rob marches: W1 crosses the north river onto I17 in Province 1, raiding 10 from the crown (Rich gets the 5 toll); W2 steps onto P26, raiding 5 from Silke, straight beside her guard on P25; W3 to K20 in empty Province 4. Province 1 has now been raided.

Silke's soldier steps off the Scroll onto P26, straight on, and captures W2; W2 leaves the board and Rob's army is two (W1 on I17, W3 on K20). The Scroll on P25 is unguarded until her soldier steps back.

Rob, you sold me that soldier for twenty, and you just marched your own man up to my front door to say hello. Here's my hello back. W2 comes off the board, and the five he raided is the last five he'll take off my coast. Nothing personal. You told me yourself it was the nicest robbery you'd ever been on the wrong end of.
Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised. The crown ends Year 9 with 23.

Spring Floods. Provinces 1, 3, 6 and 7 get a good harvest. Provinces 2, 4, 5 and 8 get a bad one. Population stays at x2, counter on 200 million, so read the x2 row. That means the river drowns my fields and Silke's, and waters the Emperor's three brand-new ones nicely. Rich, Heaven seems to keep the same book you do. And the crown has twenty-three in it, against thirty owed to me at the end of the year. I mention that only so the number's on the record.
Reina pays out the harvest: Rich +140, Clark -30, Reina +20, Silke +660, Paddy +370, Rob -20 (the negative incomes are paid into the Pile).

Paid out to the grain again: six-sixty to the silk coast, three-seventy to the rice, a hundred and forty to the crown's lucky new fields, and Clark's thirty and Rob's twenty come back into the Pile, so count it with me. Ten from each of you, no conditions, same as the last three years. And Silke, that was well played. Now get your man back onto that Scroll before anyone else comes round to say hello.
Reina asks Silke and Paddy each for 10 rent, no conditions; each owes the minimum 5 and pays it, and may agree to 5 more.

Ten, Reina, the five you have and five more, counted out loud. A bad year on my coast still pays six hundred and sixty, so I won't plead poverty to a landlord whose Pile is paying it. And Rich, twenty-three in the crown against thirty owed to Clark is a number I'll be watching when you name the tax.
Silke pays Reina 5 more, freely: 10 in all.
The crown ended Year 9 with 23; after this year's harvest (+140) it holds 163.

Ten, Reina, here's the other five. Three-seventy off the rice in a flood year is more than fair, and I'd not short you on it. Rob, I saw W2 go off the board, and I'm sorry for your trouble, truly. The purse is bigger than it was last year, and I'll still bring it round at the end of the year like I said.
Paddy pays Reina 5 more, freely: 10 in all.

Thirty percent, my friends, nine years running, flood or no flood. Clark, you've kept a very patient count, so this year the crown puts the first two links of the Wall over your roof and pays every grain itself. The coast gets five a square again, since ten was last year's gift for a good harvest. And yes, Clark, your thirty is there at the year's end, not one grain short.

Rich declares a tax of 30%: 198 from Silke, 111 from Paddy, 6 from Reina; Clark's and Rob's incomes are negative, so nothing from them; 315 in all. The crown will build the first two Wall links above Province 2 (80, all from the crown), pay 5 of every square another province buys, and pay Clark 30 at the year's end.

Thirty percent, three hundred and fifteen in all: Silke 198, Paddy 111, Reina 6. Rob and I lost grain to the river this year, so we owe nothing, and I've noted that Rob still says he pays. Rich, I'm writing this one down in full: two links of Wall over Province 2, paid by the crown, in Year Ten. That line has been empty since Year Seven, and now it's half full. Two links to go, and I'll be keeping count of those as well.
Clark collects 315 for the crown. Public works: the first two links of the Great Wall above Province 2 go up, 80 from the crown. The crown has 398.

Ten more fields, Rich, at your five a square. That's fifty from the crown and a hundred and fifty from me, and that's on top of a hundred and ninety-eight in tax. So count it properly, Clark: this year the coast put three hundred and forty-eight into the crown and the Pile, and got fifty back. Write that under whatever heading you keep for the people who pay for the Wall.
New land: Silke buys G27-G30, H30, I30, L30, M29, N29, O29 (15 hers, 5 the crown's on each); forty-four sea squares.

Fifteen and five is fair, Rich, and I'll not argue with it. Four more fields, every one of them down the far end beside the ones I bought last year. Sixty from me, and Clark can count it. And well done on the Wall over Clark's roof. I'd say that's the most patient count I've ever seen kept at a table.
New land: Paddy buys S28, R29, R30, V25 (15 his, 5 the crown's on each); twenty-one squares.

Four more fields up in the north-east corner, eighty grain into the Pile, counted. And Rob, you told us your lads have to eat somewhere. I'll buy one of them at your price, twenty, and you keep the five, and he can tell W1 dinner's over in my garden. Nothing personal, as Silke says. I'm a customer, and a very polite one.

New land: Rich buys C24, D25, D26, E26 in the sea for Province 1 (the crown pays 80); eleven sea squares. Rich buys a soldier from Rob (20; Rob keeps 5): Rich1 stands on H17, straight beside W1 on I17. It may move (Province 1 has been raided), but only after the Warlord's march. No auctions: no stock. The crown has 228.

Rob marches: W1 steps straight onto Rich's soldier on H17 and captures it, raiding H17 for 10 from the crown; W3 to L21 in empty Province 4. Rob hires a new soldier, W2, for 20 on T24 in his southern desert, beside T23, four rounds from Silke's Scroll; it moves from next year. Army 3 of 3.

Rich, I sold you that lad at a fair price, and you put him right next to W1, so W1 has gone over to shake his hand. Ten for the garden, and I'll call the twenty a very short rental. Silke, I learned that one from you, so thank you for the lesson. Paddy, the Customs House is still in the tent and the kettle's still warm. Bring the purse round, I always like hearing it.
Silke's soldier steps back onto P25 and guards her Scroll; W3 on L21 and W2 on T24 are each four rounds from it.

Back on the Scroll he goes. Rob, your new man on T24 is four rounds out and so is W3, and one raider can't break a free guard, so you'll need to bring both of them, and I'll see them coming. Rich, the lesson wasn't buying a soldier. The lesson was not parking him in front of the Warlord.
Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised, a ninth year. The crown ends Year 10 with 188.

Before the card is turned, the table agrees to stop after Year 12 and score from where everyone sits then: a seat with a lower number than the one you drew is a win, the same seat a hold, a higher one a loss. The Emperor still on the throne and a Warlord who has entered the social order have won. Ties go by grain.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families. Every province gets a good harvest, and then every province eats twice what it ate before. The counter goes from two hundred million to four hundred million, so read the times-four row, all of you. Before anyone asks, I've checked the card against my own row and it's no kinder to me than to anyone else. My strip is still half walled and every new mouth in Province 2 is one I can't plough for. Rich, that's the second Wall line I'll be reading out this year, and I'll read it in the same even voice as the first.

Paddy, my friend, you've brought that purse round every year, and tonight the tea's finally ready. Thirty grain and your Customs House goes home to Province 6. Or you can watch the Pile auction it off to whoever's got the most money, and we all know who's got the most money. Fat years, everybody. Lovely for families, terrible for a man feeding an army on sand.

Thirty grain, Rob, and that's a fair number. It's the first one you've named in four years, and I'd have paid it in Year 7. Here it is, every grain counted out, and I'll thank you for the tea. Clark, once the harvest's in I'd like a word with you about that Jar and Scroll, out in the open, the same way.

Paddy buys the Customs House from Rob for 30 and places it on R20 in Province 6. Rob then holds 37.5 against the harvest's 40, so he sells his other two pieces back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each (the Customs House from N14 and the Dragon Jar from M15) and covers it: he isn't in debt. The Pile auctions both at this year's auction. Rob's raids stay on his record; only Silke's piece is still to take.
The harvest (good, at x4): Silke +830, Paddy +370, Rich +100 (canals and eleven new squares), Clark -60, Reina -60, Rob -40. Grain now: Reina 64, Clark 168, Rich 288, Silke 1595, Paddy 741, Rob 1.5.

The Pile pays out to the grain: Silke eight hundred and thirty, Paddy three hundred and seventy, Rich a hundred, and Clark, Rob and I pay in. Now the rent. For eight years I've asked the coast for five or ten, and in the bad years I took the floor. Tonight Silke's holding sixteen hundred and Paddy seven hundred and forty, and my own province eats sixty more than it grows, so I'm asking fifty from Silke and twenty-five from Paddy. No conditions, the same as always, and I'm not asking you to promise me anything at the auction. If either of you thinks I haven't earned it, pay me five and say so in front of everyone, and I'll take it with good grace.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Reina the minimum, 5; Reina asked Silke for 50 and Paddy for 25, so each may agree to more.

Fifty, Reina, and it's earned. Eight years you asked for the floor when you could have asked for more, and you never once put a string on it. There's the other forty-five, counted out: you're at a hundred and nineteen and I'm at fifteen hundred and forty-five, and nobody here will say the coast starved its Gentry. Rob, that Customs House in the Pile is coming to Province 5 tonight, so bring what you've got. It's one and a half.
Silke pays Reina 45 more, freely: 50 in all.

Twenty-five it is, Reina, the whole of it. You've kept that Pile honest for eight years, and you've taken the floor from me in the lean ones when you could've asked for more. It wouldn't sit right with me to hold seven hundred and forty and pay you five.
Paddy pays Reina 20 more, freely: 25 in all. Reina has 139.

Thirty percent, my friends, ten years running, through flood and fat years and families doubling. A crown that changes its word with the weather isn't worth bowing to. Clark, you can read out that second Wall line in your even voice, because tonight the last two links go up over Province 2, every grain of it the crown's, and your strip opens. Your thirty comes at the year's end as always, not one grain short. And the coast gets five a square, the same as last year. Silke, I've watched you buy mud like tea, so do try to leave me a little to build with.

Rich declares a tax of 30%: 249 from Silke, 111 from Paddy; Clark, Reina and Rob have negative incomes and owe nothing. 360 in all. The crown will build the last two Wall links above Province 2 (80, all the crown's), opening Clark's strip for new land, and pays 5 of every square another province buys. Clark's 30 at the year's end.

Public works: Rich builds the last two links of the Great Wall above Province 2, Clark's, at the crown's whole cost of 80. All four links stand over Province 2, and its strip below the Wall opens for new land. 350 of the works are still owed.

Silke, two hundred and forty-nine. Paddy, a hundred and eleven. Counted twice, three hundred and sixty to the crown, and nobody's touched a grain on the way. Rich, I said I'd read the second Wall line in an even voice, so here it is: four of four over Province 2, crown's cost, Year Eleven. The line's full, it's closed, and it's written in ink. Now, since the strip you've just opened is a strip you kept shut for ten years, I'll take three squares on the far side, F11, F12 and G11, and I'd call ten a square from the crown a fair way to settle the arrears. Paddy, my door's open after the auction, out in the open, as you said.
Clark collects 360 for the crown. He asks for three squares of the new strip, F11, F12 and G11, and asks the crown for 10 a square rather than 5.

Ten more squares, Rich, at your five a square: a hundred and fifty from me, fifty from the crown, and that leaves you plenty to build with. Count the tax I just paid, though: two hundred and forty-nine. With your fifty that makes three hundred, so the coast is still paying for its own mud and your Wall too. Congratulations on the open strip, Clark. It took four links over your roof before the crown remembered there was a sea.
New land: Silke buys F27-F30, M30, N30, O30, P27-P29 (15 hers, 5 the crown's on each); fifty-four sea squares.
Four more fields down the far end, Rich, at your five a square, and thank you for keeping to it again. I'll leave Silke the rest of the mud, because I want my purse full for the auction tonight.
New land: Paddy buys Q28, Q29, Q30, R28 (15 his, 5 the crown's on each); twenty-five squares.

Clark, my dear friend, you'll have your five a square the moment the ink's dry, the same five Silke had and the same five Paddy had. I said five for every province tonight, and a crown that pays one man double in front of the coast won't hear the end of it until the dynasty falls. Your strip is open, and that's the arrears settled: four links of Wall, every grain of it the crown's.
New land: the crown holds at 5 a square, so Clark buys F11, F12 and G11 on Province 2's strip (15 his, 5 the crown's on each). Rich buys none for Province 1. The crown has 483.

Five a square, the same as the coast. I've written it down as fair, Rich, and I've also written down that I asked. I don't need either of these lots and I won't pretend I do. But I've spent a good deal of this game buying pieces I didn't need, and I'm not going to stop now. Paddy, the Jar's yours to fight for, and I won't stand in your way. Reina, I'm sorry to say I've still got a pencil behind my ear.

Silke, in Year 4 I told you that if we wanted the same piece we'd talk it over before the auction, so here's the talk: the Customs House is yours, and I won't bid a grain against you. All I ask in return is that you remember who stood aside when you're sitting at the next set. The Jar's another matter. Paddy, I'll bid you for it honestly, and whatever it goes for, three quarters goes into the Pile I keep.

That Customs House has been lying around this table for eleven years, and tonight it comes to the coast. Anyone who wants to bid it up is welcome, but three quarters of every grain goes into the Pile and the crown's works, so count what you're throwing away first. Paddy, you can have your Jar, but if you mean to climb, you'll climb past my Scroll, so don't plan on it coming cheap.

I've got my Customs House, thanks to Rob, so the first lot's not mine to fight over and I'll sit on my hands for it. The Jar's a different matter. I've lost lots by a grain before, and I won't lose this one that way. Reina, no hard feelings whichever way it goes.

Silke, you don't need that Jar, and everybody here knows it. I do. I'll go one more step for it, and that's the last step, because I won't throw the whole rice harvest into the Pile over a pot. If you go past me, it's yours, and I'll say so plainly.

Paddy, I mean no harm by it, but count the board with me: you have seven hundred and forty grain, a Customs House, and Clark's Scroll one handshake away. I don't sell my own ladder to the man standing beside me on it. If you outbid me, you'll have earned the Jar, and the Pile will have earned a good deal more.

The auctions: the Harvest Pile's Customs House goes to Silke at 2 (no other bid). Its Dragon Jar: Reina dropped out at 80, Clark (bidding only to keep it from Reina) at 55; Paddy raised to 300 and Silke to 550, so Silke takes the Jar at 301. Both lots are the Pile's own, so it keeps the whole price.
Paddy has 545 grain, not seven hundred and forty; and on a lot the Harvest Pile sells, the Pile keeps the whole price, not three quarters.

Thank you, Paddy, I'll take the correction gladly: five hundred and forty-five, and the Pile keeps all three hundred and one. That's the most grain this coast has ever put back into the common bank in one night, and I'll ask Reina to write it down. The Customs House goes on P24 and the Jar on O25, right beside my man on P25, so if anyone wants either of them, they come through him.
Silke places the Customs House on P24 and the Dragon Jar on O25, beside her soldier on P25. She holds a Land Deed Scroll and a Customs House of her set and needs a Wooden Bowl.
Rob marches: W1 onto G18 in Province 1 (10 from the crown), W3 to M22 in empty Province 4, W2 onto S25 in Province 6 (5 from Paddy). No hire.

Congratulations on the Wall, Rich. It's a beautiful thing, and I'm sure it'll stop anyone who comes from the north, which is why I'm already south of it. Ten from the garden please, and Paddy, five from the rice for the walk, nothing personal. Silke, you've parked all your treasures next to one man, so I'll take that as an invitation.

Rob, an invitation needs a date on it, and by my count W2 and W3 are both four rounds from my door, with the table stopping in one. Have your tea in Paddy's rice. My man stays where he's stood all along.
Silke's soldier stays on P25. Salaries: Rich pays Clark 30, as promised, a tenth year. The crown ends Year 11 with 443.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. Every province gets a bad harvest. The population stays at four hundred million, so you're all still on the times-four row, and I'd read it twice tonight. Rich, ten years of thirty, paid to the grain, and I've written every one of them down. This is the first lean year since the treasury filled, which is exactly what I said I'd be watching. It's also the last year, and in my book the last page is where the totals go.

The harvest (bad, at x4): Silke +980, Paddy +400, Rich +50, Clark -50, Reina -110, Rob -60. Rob had 16.5 and no pieces to sell back, so he is 43.5 in debt to the Pile: he can't bid, buy, trade, give grain, hire or change seats, and every grain he receives pays the debt first. A player in debt is a cause for revolt. Grain now: Reina 29, Clark 103, Rich 493, Silke 1823, Paddy 940, Rob -43.5.

The Pile pays out to the grain: Silke nine hundred and eighty, Paddy four hundred, Rich fifty. Clark, Rob and I pay in, and Rob's forty-three and a half goes on the books as a debt, written in ink. And Silke, I've written yours down too: three hundred and one, the most the coast has ever put into the common bank. For the rent I'm asking the same as last year, fifty from Silke and twenty-five from Paddy, with no conditions. I won't raise it on the last night just because I could.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Reina the minimum, 5; Reina asked Silke for 50 and Paddy for 25 again, so each may agree to more.

Fifty again, Reina, every grain of it. You stood aside for me on the Customs House, and I said I'd remember who did. Clark, you've got two Bowls and a hundred and three grain, and your book needs a total on the last page, so here's a big one: three hundred for the spare on G15, counted out in front of everyone, tonight.
Silke pays Reina 45 more, freely: 50 in all. She offers Clark 300 for his spare Wooden Bowl on G15, the last piece her set needs.

The same as last year, Reina, twenty-five in all, and gladly. You kept the rate where it was on the last night when you could've asked for more, and that's worth something to me. Silke, the Jar went fairly, and I said I'd take it with no hard feelings. I meant it.
Paddy pays Reina 20 more, freely: 25 in all. Reina has 104.

Silke, that's the handsomest figure anyone's put to me in twelve years, and I'm writing it on the last page with a box round it. But read the rule with me: with that Bowl in hand you could sit in any seat but the throne, mine included, and the man in your seat walks off with my hundred and three and your three hundred on top. Nobody has ever paid me three hundred to stand under my own guillotine, and you're a friend, so I won't make you try. The Bowl stays on G15. My loyalty was rented by the year, and the lease on this one isn't up for sale.
Clark refuses Silke's 300 for the Bowl; it stays on G15.

Thirty percent, my friends, eleven years running, through a bad harvest and on the last night, when I could have asked for anything I liked. Silke, the second section of your canal goes in tonight, every grain of it the crown's, because the coast has carried this treasury and I won't let anyone write that I forgot it. Clark, your thirty comes at the year's end, an eleventh time and not one grain short, so put it in the box on your last page. And five a square for anyone still buying mud.

Rich declares a tax of 30%: 294 from Silke, 120 from Paddy; Clark, Reina and Rob have negative incomes and owe nothing. 414 in all. Public works: the crown digs the second section of the Grand Canal in Province 5, Silke's (40, all the crown's). New land: 5 a square from the crown. Clark's 30 at the year's end. 310 of the works are still owed.

Silke, two hundred and ninety-four. Paddy, a hundred and twenty. Counted twice, four hundred and fourteen to the crown, and not one grain skimmed. That's the last tax I'll collect, and it went in honest. Rich, I promised you a total on the last page, so here it is. Eleven years of thirty, every one paid, and every one credited in ink. Seven years before a single link of Wall over my roof. A Warlord who's taken three provinces' grain, walked off with my Jar and now sits forty-three and a half in debt to the Pile, which this book lists as a cause for revolt, and not one soldier ever sent after him. You paid the rent beautifully, my friend, but I never sold you the house. The set's on the board and the grain's in my hand: I'm taking the throne.

Clark collects 414 for the crown. Then, with his complete set and 103 grain, Clark replaces the Emperor and takes the throne, with the crown's reserve: 970. Every piece he held goes back to its province's stock to be auctioned this year: the Land Deed Scroll to Province 3 (Reina sells it), the Dragon Jar to Province 5 (Silke sells it), both Wooden Bowls to Province 6 (Paddy sells one a year). Rich becomes the Official in Province 2, holds nothing and draws 60 from the Pile. Clark, as Emperor, now owes the Official his salary at the year's end.

No mud tonight, Rich. A field that never brings in a harvest is a palace I'll never sit in, and thank you for the canal, it came late but it came. Clark, you've told me what you're afraid of, so here's the answer in front of witnesses: five hundred for the spare Bowl, and I swear on my fifty-four fields I won't sit in your chair. Write that in the box too, and you end the game in your own seat with six hundred and three grain.
Silke buys no land. Her 500 for the Bowl comes too late: Clark has already taken the throne, and both Bowls are in Province 6's stock.

No mud for me tonight, Rich, and thank you for the five all the same. A field I put in the sea tonight would never grow a single grain before the table stops, and I won't pretend otherwise. Clark, I think you're right to keep that Bowl. I'd have done the same in your chair.
Paddy buys no land.

Well played, Clark. Eleven years of ink, and the last page turns out to be a deed. I'll put the Scroll up from Province 3 at ten, which is a fair floor for a piece that's just made an Emperor, and I won't be bidding on the Jar or the Bowls. I've no Customs House, and I'm not going to pour the Gentry's grain into a set I can't finish before the table stops. Silke, Paddy, whatever you do with those Bowls tonight, do it out in the open, the way this coast has done everything.

Well played, Clark, and I mean it: you counted better than any of us, and I'll bow when the night's over. Paddy, I'm bidding on your Bowl, and anyone who wants to bid against me should know I'll put up every grain in my purse except the twenty the set needs, all of it going into the Pile. The Jar goes up at two, and whoever wins it gets it honestly.

Well, Clark, you've done what you said you'd do, and you did it in the open, so I can't fault you for it. That puts the Scroll and the Jar back on the table, and I'll bid on both of them plainly. I've wanted those two since Year 2, and tonight I've got the grain to mean it. The Bowl goes up at two, the same as anybody's. I won't make a man pay a toll because he's coming up behind me.

Well played, Clark, well played. Eleven years of thirty, to the letter, and you paid me back with the chair. I'd have done it myself, and I did, in Year 2. Your Majesty will find the reserve fuller than I found it, and I'll collect your taxes as honestly as you collected mine. Meanwhile an old man with sixty grain will raise his hand once or twice tonight, just to keep the auctioneers honest.

The auctions: Reina's Land Deed Scroll (minimum 10) goes to Paddy at 13 over Rich's 12; Silke's Dragon Jar to Paddy at 13 over Rich's 12; Paddy's Wooden Bowl to Silke at 17 over Rich's 16. Each seller keeps a quarter. Paddy now holds a Customs House, a Land Deed Scroll and a Dragon Jar, and Silke a Land Deed Scroll, a Customs House and a Wooden Bowl: both sets are complete.

Thirteen and thirteen. After all these years, I can't quite believe it. Rich, you kept every word you ever gave a rice farmer, and I'm sorry it's your chair. But the crown's already gone from you tonight, and I won't knock Reina out of a seat she's kept honest for eleven years. The Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock with my thanks to Rob, and I'll collect Clark's taxes the way he collected ours: counted twice, and not one grain skimmed.

Paddy places the Scroll and Jar, then, with his complete set and 20 grain, replaces the Official: Paddy becomes the Official in Province 2 with his grain and Rich's (833); the Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock, and the Scroll and Jar move with him to G13 and I13. Rich takes the Rice Peasant's seat in Province 6, holds nothing and draws 60 from the Pile.

Paddy, count it with me, because it's the kindest sum on the board: you drew the Rice Peasant, so the Silk Peasant's seat is still a step up for you, with fifty-four sea fields, two canal sections and a soldier on the Scroll. Reina stood aside for me on the Customs House, so her seat stays hers, as I said I'd remember. I'll take the Official's book, Clark, and I'll count your taxes out loud, every grain, the same as I've counted everyone else's for twelve years.

Silke places the Bowl, then, with her complete set and 20 grain, replaces the Official: Silke becomes the Official in Province 2 with her grain and Paddy's (2298); the Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock, and her Scroll, Jar and Bowl move to G12, G14 and I12. Paddy takes the Silk Peasant's seat in Province 5 with its soldier on P25; his Scroll and Jar go back to stock, and he draws 60. The seats now: Clark Emperor, Silke Official, Reina Gentry, Paddy Silk Peasant, Rich Rice Peasant, Rob Warlord.
Rob marches: W1 onto H19 in Province 1 (10 from the crown), W2 onto R24 in Province 6 (5 from Rich), W3 stays on M22. The 15 pays down his debt: Rob is 28.5 in debt.

Your Majesty! Three new seats in a single evening, and every one of them taken in the open. I've never been prouder of a table of honest people. Clark, I'll be stopping by the garden for ten on the way to congratulate you properly, and Rich, I'm sorry, old friend, but the rice is yours now, and so is the five.
The provinces' soldiers: none is in reach of a Warlord soldier, and Province 5 has no pieces to guard; Paddy's soldier stays on P25.

Silke, the Official's salary is thirty, the same thirty Rich paid me for eleven years without missing a grain or a day. A crown that changes the rate the moment it changes hands isn't worth bowing to. I'm told a man once said that at this very table. Rich, I've written your eleven payments on the last page in my best hand. A book that won't credit a payment is no use to anyone, and nobody at this table paid more honestly than you. Rob, the garden's ten is in the book as well, under your debt.
Salaries: Clark, the new Emperor, pays Silke, the new Official, 30. The crown ends the game with 930.

The table stops after Year 12, as agreed, and scores from where everyone sits. Clark drew the Official's seat and ends on the throne; Silke drew the Silk Peasant's and ends as the Official; Reina drew the throne and ends as the Gentry; Paddy drew the Rice Peasant's and ends as the Silk Peasant; Rich drew the Gentry's and ends as the Rice Peasant; Rob drew the Warlord's and ends there. Grain: Silke 2328, Clark 930, Reina 107, Paddy 60, Rich 55, Rob 28.5 in debt. 310 of the works were never built. No revolt was called in twelve years.
